title: I Set My Rainbow in the Cloud — Blood, a Bow, a Drunken Man
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. In the last lesson we watched the waters go down, and Noah came out of the ship, and the very first thing he did was build an altar. God smelled that pleasant aroma, and he said in his heart: I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake. Today, in this lesson, God is going to take that sentence spoken inside his own heart and turn it into a covenant you can see.

And the question this lesson puts to you is this: the God you carry in your heart — is he a God who is always one moment away from going off, or is he a God who has already hung his weapon up and sworn a covenant?

Let me put the answer at the very front: the rainbow is not a placebo hung in the sky for human beings to look at. Verse 16 says, "I will look at it, that I may remember" — and the subject of that sentence is God. This sign is set up on God's side of the covenant, and the guarantor of this covenant, from beginning to end, is he.
1. The Commission Re-issued After the Flood
Verse 1: "God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, 'Be fruitful, multiply, and replenish the earth.'"

Brothers and sisters, you have heard that sentence before. It is the same sentence God spoke to Adam and Eve in 1:28. After the flood, God issues the original commission all over again. He did not shrink the human calling because human beings had failed once.

But something has changed, and the text records it very honestly. Verse 2 says, "The fear of you and the dread of you will be on every animal of the earth, and on every bird of the sky." The word used in 1:28 was "have dominion", רָדָה (*radah*); here it has been swapped for "fear" and "dread" — מוֹרָא וְחַת (*mora vechat*). The relationship between humanity and the created order has moved from stewardship to tension.
Verse 3 then adds a new permission: "Every moving thing that lives will be food for you." In 1:29 what God gave human beings was the green herb; only here is meat added to the table.
And then verse 4 is the one and only restriction inside that whole grant of permission: "But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat."

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the shape of this — it is exactly the shape of chapter 2. Chapter 2: you may eat from the whole garden, only not from one tree. Chapter 9: you may eat every living thing that moves, only not the blood. What God gives is always an overwhelming freedom, plus one clearly drawn line. That little word "but" — אַךְ (*ach*) — is how God has always worked.
After the flood God said, "Every moving thing that lives will be food for you." Does that make vegetarianism unbiblical?

No. Genesis 9:3 is God widening the range; it is not God issuing a command. And Romans 14 settles the matter plainly: "One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables. Don't let him who eats despise him who doesn't eat. Don't let him who doesn't eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him." In other words, eating and not eating are both free; judging is the problem. So a Christian may choose to eat no meat for the sake of health, for the sake of the environment, out of mercy towards animals, or as a personal discipline — and that is a good thing. What he may not do is turn it into a measure of salvation or a ranking of spiritual maturity. The line that actually has to be kept is the one the same passage draws next: the blood may not be eaten — because the life is in the blood, and life belongs to God.
2. The Life Is in the Blood
The word "blood", דָּם (*dam*), occurs seven times in chapter 9. It is the theme-word of the whole chapter.
Why may the blood not be eaten? Verse 4 gives its own answer — "flesh with its life, that is, its blood." Leviticus 17:11 says it more fully: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood."

Brothers and sisters, the meaning of this boundary is not dietary hygiene. It is sovereignty. God hands the whole animal kingdom over into human hands, and in the same breath he says: the life is not yours. You may use it — but the ownership of life does not sit with you.
Then verse 6 pushes that principle up from the animals onto human beings: "Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image."

In Hebrew the very shape of this verse is a law in itself: "sheds", שֹׁפֵךְ (*shofekh*), is active; "will be shed", יִשָּׁפֵךְ (*yishafekh*), is passive; the two halves stand face to face like a mirror. What you do to a person comes back on you in the same form.

But the half of the verse you must take hold of is the second one: "for God made man in his own image." Brothers and sisters, the first thing this verse is protecting is not a scale of penalties — it is the image in a human being. A human life is inviolable not because a person is outstanding, not because he is useful, not because he contributes something; it is because every single person carries that image.

So James 3:9 says, "With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God." Brothers and sisters, the apostle ties cursing a person straight back to this verse. That person you criticised in the group chat today, that person you quietly look down on — every one of them carries that image. Touch him, and you are touching the One whom that image represents.
"Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man" — does this verse support the death penalty?

The verse really has been used to argue that question down the centuries, and both sides quote it. Those in favour read it as God authorising human society to deal with the crime of murder. Those against point out that this is a declaration inside a narrative rather than a statute in a criminal code, and that the New Testament says "don't seek revenge yourselves" and that mercy triumphs over judgement. These notes will not settle the question from the pulpit on behalf of either side, and they add this reminder: the real force of this verse is not in the penalty, it is in the reason — "for God made man in his own image." That is to say, the horror of killing a person is that it destroys a being who carries the image of God. Whatever position you hold on capital punishment, this one sentence requires all of us to weigh every single human life as something immense.
If "the life is in the blood", may Christians give blood or receive a transfusion today?

Yes. What chapter 9 forbids is eating flesh with its blood, and what it is teaching is reverence — life belongs to God, and it is not to be swallowed as food. A transfusion gives life to a person; the direction is exactly the opposite. It preserves life; it does not consume life. When Acts 15 asks the Gentile believers to abstain "from what is strangled, and from blood", it is handling the same matter — reverence at the table, and the conscience of the Jewish believers of that time. To read this verse as a prohibition on the medical use of blood is to take a principle of reverence and misapply it to an act that saves a life. In fact, giving blood is itself a picture of the very thing Leviticus said: blood is what covers and rescues a life.
3. A Light from the Original: a Bow Hung Up
Verses 8 to 17 are the summit of this chapter, and they are the first covenant the Bible records from beginning to end.
Verse 13: "I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth."

Brothers and sisters, the word for "rainbow" in Hebrew is קֶשֶׁת (*qeshet*). And everywhere else this word turns up in the Old Testament, it means almost without exception a bow — the bow you go to war with. When Esau is told to take his bow, it is this word. When David sings that the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, it is this word.
So when a Hebrew heard, "I set my קֶשֶׁת in the cloud", what came up in his mind was not a lovely band of seven colours. It was a weapon.

And picture for a moment the way that bow hangs in the sky: the curve of its back arching upward, both its tips pointing down. If that bow were strung and an arrow were fitted to it, where would the arrow fly? Straight up into heaven.

Brothers and sisters, God has hung his bow up, and the direction he has hung it is towards himself. This is the first time in the Bible that God, in some fashion, takes upon himself the consequence of a broken covenant. And thousands of years later that arrow really was loosed — and it struck his own Son.

Verses 15 and 16 say it twice over, one after the other: "I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you"; "I will look at it, that I may remember." Brothers and sisters, take hold of the subject of those sentences. The sign is for God to see; it is not for people to see. You do not have to run outside every time it rains to hunt for that arc in the sky. The dependability of this covenant is not built on whether you saw it.

And one more thing: how wide does this covenant reach? Verse 10 says it is made "with every living creature that is with you"; verse 16 speaks of "every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth." Four times over the text says "all flesh" — even the beasts of the field are inside this covenant. This is the first covenant in the Bible, and its reach is the widest of them all. Your neighbour who does not believe in the Lord still has his spring sowing and his autumn harvest today. In theology we call this common grace.
"I set my rainbow in the cloud" — but a rainbow is a natural phenomenon anyway. What kind of miracle is that?

The text never says that the rainbow came into existence on that day. What it says is that God "set" something already there into the cloud and gave it a new meaning. And the Hebrew word for "rainbow" (קֶשֶׁת) simply is the word for "bow" — the bow that is a weapon. This matters: God hangs the bow up, with the string turned towards himself and the back of it turned towards us. The gods of the ancient Near East were forever shooting arrows at people; this God has put his bow away. So the weight of this sign does not lie in the physics of it, it lies in who is aimed at whom. And this is how signs have always worked in Scripture: water, bread, a cup — every one of them an everyday thing, and once God sets it inside a covenant it carries meaning. Every time you see the rainbow, what you are seeing is a God who no longer has his bow aimed at you.
Verse 16 says that God "looks and remembers." Is the sign for God to see, or for people to see?

What the text says is, "I will look at it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth." The subject is God. And that is a great comfort: the keeping of this covenant does not depend on human beings being able to remember. People forget, people doubt, people are frightened when the rain comes — and God says, I will look at it and I will remember. Of course a person is comforted when he sees it too; but the ground of that comfort is God's own faithfulness, not our memory and not our feelings. The Lord's Supper in the New Testament has the same two sides — "do this in memory of me", and at the same time a covenant the Lord himself instituted and himself sustains. So the next time your faith is weak, remember this: the force of the covenant does not rest on your side.
4. A Righteous Man Falls in a Vineyard
The passage that comes next is very hard to read, and Scripture does not cover over one single word of it on his behalf.
Verses 20 and 21: "Noah began to be a farmer, and planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and got drunk. He was uncovered within his tent."

Brothers and sisters, please put that verse next to everything that came before it: 6:8 says he found favour; 6:9 says he was a righteous man, blameless, and that he walked with God; chapter 7 says he did it all exactly as he was told, without altering a thing; chapter 8 says the first thing he did on coming out of the ship was build an altar.
And then, in chapter 9, he is lying there drunk, with nothing on.

Scripture never retouches its saints. And this matters enormously for pastoral work: however glorious a person's past may be, none of it guarantees his next step. 1 Corinthians 10:12 says, "Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn't fall." And notice where the fall takes place — not in the flood, but in the vineyard. The slackening off that comes once the crisis is over is very often more dangerous than the crisis itself.

Verse 22: "Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brothers outside." The text spends a single sentence on what Ham did: he saw, and then he went outside and talked.

And then the writer gives a whole verse, filmed in very slow motion, to what the other two did: "Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it on both their shoulders, went in backwards, and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were backwards, and they didn't see their father's nakedness."

Brothers and sisters — they went in backwards. What a beautiful thing that action is. They did not shut their eyes and rush in at speed; they walked in slowly, backwards, step by step. Because if you are going to cover another person's shame, the first thing you must spend is your own convenience.

1 Peter 4:8 says, "love covers a multitude of sins." This passage is the picture of that sentence. When you see somebody else's shame, which direction do your feet go? Outwards — or backwards, inwards?
Noah drunk and uncovered — why was this passage written into the Bible at all?

Because the Bible never prettifies its people. Here is a righteous man who has just brought his whole household through the flood and built an altar and offered sacrifice; he comes out of the ship, plants a vineyard, and then drinks himself unconscious. It was written down not so that we could discuss him, but so that we would know two things. First, being saved is not the same as being an overcomer; past experience guarantees nothing about tomorrow's footing. Second, a fall happens most often in the place where a person has let go — not in the flood, but in the vineyard. So the most dangerous season is usually not hardship; it is the days just after everything has settled down. For anyone who is still standing, this passage is a warning. For anyone who has already fallen, it is a comfort — Scripture did not strike the fallen man off the list.
Ham saw his father's nakedness and was cursed for it. Isn't that far too heavy?

Start with what the text itself says: the one cursed is Canaan, not Ham. And the words the text uses of Ham are that he "saw … and told his two brothers outside" — the problem is not that he saw, the problem is that he went out and talked. What Shem and Japheth did stands there as the contrast: they went in backwards, laid the garment across their shoulders, covered their father, and kept their faces turned away. So what this passage is really about is this — when you see somebody else's shame, do you cover it or do you spread it? As for why the curse falls on Canaan, the text does not explain, the commentators have several guesses, and we are under no obligation to supply a reason on Scripture's behalf. And one thing has to be stated plainly: this passage has been gravely misused in history to give cover to slavery and to racial discrimination. That is a total distortion of the text, and we must reject it in so many words.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first, and the one that has to be handled with the greatest seriousness: taking "the curse of Ham" and using it to support racial discrimination in any form whatsoever. Read the text properly — the one cursed in verse 25 is Canaan, not Ham, not the whole of Ham's posterity, and certainly not a skin colour. Canaan's descendants are listed plainly in chapter 10 as the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, and what this oracle points to is the situation Israel met when it came into that land. In recent centuries some have identified the descendants of Ham with the peoples of Africa and then used this verse to underwrite the keeping of slaves; on the text, that has not a leg to stand on. This is a passage that has been misused, and the preacher must stand up and say so himself from the pulpit; he may not go around it. Galatians 3:28 is where the matter ends.

The second is preaching the rainbow as a piece of psychological reassurance for human beings. Verse 16 says, "I will look at it, that I may remember", and the subject is God. If you preach it as "seeing a rainbow will make you feel a little easier", you have taken the weight out of the covenant, and what the congregation leans on becomes their own feelings instead of the faithfulness of God.

The third is skating lightly over Noah's drunkenness. Some, wanting to protect "the image of the Bible's characters", reach this point and dispose of it in one sentence. But Scripture itself did not skip it. Skip it, and the congregation will come away imagining that past a certain level of spirituality a person stops falling — and that is the most dangerous illusion there is.

The fourth is taking "you shall not eat the blood" and spinning it out into a whole system of dietary regulations. The point of verse 4 is that life belongs to God; it is not the founding of a recipe book. Acts 15 keeps this one item chiefly for the sake of unity between Jewish and Gentile believers, not in the service of legalism. What the congregation should carry out of the door is a reverence for life, not a few more rules.

The fifth is treating verse 6 straight off as a debating motion on capital punishment. This verse really is where a great many discussions of the death penalty begin, and godly believers hold differing views on the subject. But you must notice this: the centre of gravity of the whole verse is in its second half — because God made man in his own image. If, when you have finished preaching, the congregation remembers only the punishment and does not remember that image, you have swung the axis of this verse out of true.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: the thing a Chinese family is best at is making sure that family shame is never aired in public — is that the same thing Shem and Japheth did when they covered their father? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be sorted out very carefully, or people will get hurt. Here is what is the same: neither of them is in favour of carrying a family member's humiliation outside and talking about it. Here is what is different — the motive, and the direction. What Shem and Japheth covered was one moment of weakness in their father; that is the protection of a person's dignity. But "family shame must not be aired" is very often used to cover up harm that has gone on for years — domestic violence, sexual abuse, money owed and never repaid — and that is the protection of the one doing the harm. Let me say it as plainly as I can: covering a person's humiliation is love; covering up a crime is not love, it is complicity. And the way to tell the two apart is very simple. If this thing goes on being covered, who is being protected? Who goes on being hurt? If the answer is that the one doing the harm is protected and the one being harmed goes on being harmed, then it must be spoken — and it must be spoken into the right ears.

The second question: verse 6 says, "Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man" — does that mean the family of a victim ought to go and collect the debt themselves? My answer is no. What this verse sets up is a public, authorised order of justice; it is not a licence for private revenge. Romans 12:19 puts it beyond doubt: "Don't seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God's wrath." And in Chinese culture, taking revenge and getting justice are very often welded together into a single family duty, which makes this verse very easy to misread as the Bible's endorsement of it. Please keep three things apart: pursuing justice is right; pursuing it through proper process is right; taking it into your own hands is not. Lamech's seventy-sevenfold in chapter 4 is where private revenge ends up.
7. Living 321 Out — What Is in Your Hand Is a Garment, Not a Stone
Brothers and sisters, let us now tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Shem and Japheth took a garment and went in backwards. And in John 8, when the woman caught in the act of adultery is brought in front of the Lord Jesus, what the crowd has in its hands is stones; the Lord Jesus stoops down and writes on the ground, and at the end he says, "Neither do I condemn you." Brothers and sisters, my example is very concrete: what he has in his hand is a garment, not a stone.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter hands us two utterly clear standards: life belongs to God, and human beings carry the image of God. Put those two together and you have the Bible's way of looking at a person. If you genuinely keep those two, what you say online will change; the way you talk in a meeting room about a colleague who is not present will change; and the way you treat the one person at home who gives you the most trouble will change as well.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the rainbow is a sign, and the function of a sign is to remind. One of the things the Holy Spirit does inside us is to make us remember at the moment when remembering is needed. John 14:26 says that the Holy Spirit "will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you."

Let Jesus be King — verse 6 says that sovereignty over life is in God's hand. And the most everyday application of that is this: even my right to pass judgement on another person has to be handed back to him. Brothers and sisters, that person you most want to throw a stone at — has it ever occurred to you that you were never given the authorisation?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice how lopsided this covenant is. Across the whole ten verses the human beings do nothing at all; there are no conditions, and not one sentence begins "if you …". From beginning to end it is "I establish", "I set", "I will remember." In front of a covenant like that, a person can only give thanks.

Establish God's system — what God makes with Noah is an "everlasting covenant", and the parties to it are "every living creature of all flesh." Brothers and sisters, this covenant takes in the whole created order, not one nation, not one church, not one denomination. So if you are going to establish God's system, your field of vision has to be that wide. A church that looks after nobody but its own does not look like the God of this chapter.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on selflessness, and this chapter gives it a very concrete shape: selflessness is not an abstract attitude of mind, it is that backwards walk of Shem and Japheth. The concrete shape of selflessness is that I am willing to spend my own convenience in order to keep another person's dignity intact. Put it the other way round: if a man can talk beautifully about selflessness and is always the first to pass on somebody else's embarrassment, then he has not yet arrived at this chapter.
How do you tell "covering" apart from "concealing sin"? Should things that happen inside a church be talked about?

It turns on three things. First, motive: covering protects that person's dignity; concealing protects your own face, or the organisation's. Second, truth: covering is not the same as pretending nothing happened, and what has to be faced still gets faced — what Shem and Japheth covered was their father's body, and when Noah woke up the matter was still dealt with. Third, safety: if the thing involves a crime, or violence, or someone being harmed, then it is not within the range of covering at all — it must be reported and the one harmed must be protected, and that is what Scripture requires when it says that innocent blood may not be shed. So the rule is perfectly clear: with weakness, cover; with crime, act. A church that gets those two the wrong way round will wound the weakest person in the room.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Bow Hung Up
Brothers and sisters, one and the same rainbow falls into four kinds of heart, and what each of them sees is not the same thing.

The proud heart sees: "Well, at least I'm not Ham." The easiest thing for this heart to do with the chapter is to rank the three brothers and then set itself down on the side of Shem and Japheth. Brothers and sisters, notice who it is that falls in this chapter — the righteous man who spent a hundred years building the ship, who found favour, who walked with God. If you finish reading and can think only of other people's failures, then you have not yet heard what this chapter is saying to you.

The fearful heart sees: "What if one day God changes his mind again?" This heart hears the promise and still does not quite dare to believe it. To a heart like that I want to say: look at which side the sign is hung on. Verse 16 says, "I will look at it, that I may remember." Your safety is not built on whether you remember. It is built on the fact that he sees.

The ashamed heart sees: "I am the one lying there with nothing on." Perhaps there was something humiliating in your life that somebody saw and somebody passed on, and ever since then you have not been able to lift your head in church. Brothers and sisters, look at that garment. In chapter 3 God made coats of skin with his own hands; in chapter 9 Shem and Japheth took a garment and went in backwards. The way Scripture deals with nakedness has always been to cover it, never to display it. And if there is nobody beside you bringing a garment, remember that the One who died for you has already clothed you.

The wounded heart sees: "And what about the man who told everyone about me?" There really is a man in this chapter who did that, and the text offers him no defence. I want to tell you two things. First, God saw it, and he has entered it in the account. Second — and this sentence is hard, but I am going to say it anyway — you have the chance to decide which kind of person you are going to be. The one who has been talked about knows better than anyone how much it hurts, which makes him the most qualified man in the room to become the one who walks in backwards.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, if this week you come to know something humiliating about somebody, practise walking in backwards once. Do not repeat it, do not hint at it, and do not say it out loud in the prayer meeting under cover of asking for prayer. And then think about this: what is the one practical thing I can do for him?

Second, pick one person you look down on in your heart, and write down three concrete pieces of evidence that the image of God is on him. Not to make yourself feel better — actually go and look for them. And once you have found them, pray for him once.

Third, check where it is that you let go. Noah did not fall in the flood; he fell in the vineyard. This week, write down your own "vineyard" — the setting after the crisis has passed, once you have relaxed, where things are most likely to go wrong — and then set one boundary for it.

Fourth, the next time you see a rainbow, or it simply begins to rain, do one small exercise: say to yourself, "He has seen it, and he remembers." Set the direction of the sign the right way round — it hangs on his side.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. One: in the original language of the Bible, the rainbow simply is the word for a bow, the weapon you go to war with. Two: God says, I set my bow in the cloud — and the direction that bow is pointing is towards himself. Three: and so I came to understand that this is not a romantic pattern in the sky; it is a God saying, "I will carry this account myself."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the guarantor of this covenant is God himself and not me; my safety is not built on whether I remember.
I declare that every single person carries the image of God — including the one person I find hardest to bear.
I declare that when I see another person's humiliation I will walk in backwards, with a garment in my hand and not a stone.
I declare that I am standing today not because I am strong enough; I will draw a line for myself in the very place where I am most relaxed.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be that bow hanging in the cloud.
The flood is over. The earth has sound again, and smell again, and a farmer and a vineyard again. And the last thing God does is to hang his weapon up and say: I will look at it, that I may remember.

And notice this: the drunkenness of verse 21 happens after the covenant of verse 17. Which is to say, God made the covenant first, and the man fell straight afterwards. And that covenant was not cancelled over it — not once.

Brothers and sisters, this is the order of grace. God does not wait until you have proved that you can stand before he gives you a covenant; knowing perfectly well that you will fall, he hangs the bow up first. He said it himself in 8:21: "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." He has not overestimated you. He made that covenant in full knowledge of exactly what you are.
And that bow aimed up at heaven was, in the end, really drawn. Isaiah 53 says, "Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all." That arrow was not loosed at us. It struck him.

The focus is not on whether I stood this time, not on what other people make of my humiliation, and not on whether I happened to catch sight of that arc in the sky today. The focus is on Jesus — he is the God who took the arrow. No longer I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us, that this week we would carry a garment in our hands and not a stone, and that in the very place where we are most relaxed we would still be watchful. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ The original word for "rainbow" simply is the word for "bow", and it is hung up, turned towards God himself. Does that picture change your impression of "the wrath of God"?
2. ★★★ Verse 16 says, "I will look at it, that I may remember." On whom does the keeping of this covenant rest? Why does that matter so much?
3. ★ The reason the text gives for the horror of killing a person is "for God made man in his own image." How does that reason affect the way you look at the people you do not like?
4. ★★ Noah stood firm in the flood and fell in the vineyard. What is that contrast meant to remind us of?

Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it out loud, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I would never fall the way he did), fearful (afraid that one day I will go down too), ashamed (I have already gone down), wounded (my weakness was passed around by somebody else). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ The last time you came to know about someone else's weakness, did you cover it or did you pass it on? What was the real motive in your heart at the time?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "My 'vineyard' right now — the place where I most easily let go — is this …"
9. ★★ This week, what boundary are you going to set for that place where you easily let go? Say it concretely; do not just say, "I'll be careful."

Leader's reminder: question seven will touch the wound of having been talked about. If someone mentions something that once happened inside this group, do not confront it on the spot; deal with it privately after the meeting. If a crime is involved or someone has been harmed, it must be reported as the rules require and the one harmed must be protected; "covering" may never be used as a reason to conceal it.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home this week, is there one person whose weakness you are going to choose to cover? Say what you are going to do.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, at school or in a group chat, is there one piece of gossip you are going to let stop with you?

12. ★★★ The once-a-day practice: this week, before you pass on anything about another person, ask yourself first, "Am I saying this to protect him, or to consume him?" Say which setting you most often need that question in.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the "vineyard" you named in question nine, and ask him to check on you once on the seventh day. Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: the rainbow in the Bible is, in the original language, a bow — and it is hung up. Second: that God says, "I will look at it, that I may remember" — the sign is there for him to see. Third: and so I believe in a God who does not hold his bow aimed at people. Write down here and now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one boundary you are going to set this week, and who you are going to tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep us watchful in the settled days, and to make us the kind of brother who covers another person.
